title_guess: Lending-rate benchmarks in India: bargained rates, PLR, BPLR and base rate
recurring_cast: pink box holding four bank icons
dotted arrows between the RBI coin and the four banks
two goal chips: transparency and standardisation
running_examples: one bank, one borrower: loan grows 10 lakh -> 20 lakh while the bank's rate tag is bargained down 15% -> 12% -> 7% -> 5% toward the borrower's 5%
one bank, four borrowers under PLR paying 5%, 15%, 12% and 3%
2010 review: 77% of all bank lending was below BPLR

best_moments.why: bargaining shown as a stack of struck-out rate tags climbing above the bank (15, 12, 7, then 5) while the borrower's own 5% tag stays put: negotiation as a visible tug toward one number
one bank beside four identical people, each wearing a different % tag: 'no standard rate' made obvious without reading

the two goal chips set up earlier (transparency, standardisation) get red crosses once the 77% data lands; at 410 the same chips get blue ticks under the base rate: problem and fix on the same objects

the BPLR picture is reused for base rate: the [FIXED] tag goes, one bank is ringed in gold ('sets its own'), and the dotted arrows now run from banks to RBI instead of RBI to banks: the change of authority is visible as a flipped arrow
a timeline strip stays docked at the top all video and gains ticks (1973, 2003, 2010, 2015) with dotted drop lines to each new heading: every concept is anchored to its year

weak_moments.why: the PLR definition is an italic paragraph under the picture that only repeats what the four tags already show
BPLR is defined by a three-line text paragraph before any picture appears
the 77% finding and its reason are text lines; the main evidence of the video is never drawn
base-rate calculation is a four-bullet list (fund cost, running cost, minimum return, CRR cost) with no picture of parts adding up to a rate

segments.teaches: before benchmark rates, a bank and a borrower bargained the loan rate one to one; a big or strong borrower could push it down

elements.what: yellow strip docked at the top: a 1970s band and a 2003 tick
classical bank building with a rupee coin on top
standing person (borrower)
bank -> person arrow labelled loan, amount written above it
yellow sticky % tags pinned on the bank (15%) and on the person (5%)
bank's rate struck and rewritten higher up each time: 15% -> 12% -> 7% -> 5%
loan amount 10 lakh struck and replaced by 20 lakh

segments.notes: 4 change events (~every 16 s). The struck rates are kept on screen as a ladder, so the history of the bargain stays visible. The top timeline strip is the video's era marker and never leaves.
segments.idea: in the old system each loan rate was settled by bargaining, so stronger borrowers paid less
segments.shown_as: a bank lends to a person along a 'loan' arrow; both get a yellow % tag (bank 15%, person 5%); as the loan amount is struck from 10 lakh to 20 lakh, the bank's tag is struck and rewritten lower again and again (15 -> 12 -> 7 -> 5) until it meets the person's 5%
segments.example: loan 10 lakh -> 20 lakh; bank rate 15% -> 12% -> 7% -> 5%; borrower asks 5%

segments.teaches: under the Prime Lending Rate system (from 1973 on the strip) each bank used its own discretion, so different customers paid very different rates; the system lacked transparency and standardisation

elements.what: PLR, with a hand-drawn pointer adding its full name
light-blue band holding one bank and four people in a row
four identical standing people, each with its own green % tag (5, 15, 12, 3)
italic definition under the band, the word 'discretion' in blue
red 'issues' label with two cream chips: no transparency, no standardisation
1973 tick added at the left end of the top strip

segments.notes: 5 change events (~every 10 s). The four different tags on four identical people are the real argument; the paragraph repeats it. Verify before reuse: the strip dates the start of PLR to 1973; check this date against a reliable source.
segments.idea: under PLR every bank set its own benchmark, so borrowers paid scattered rates and nobody could compare
segments.shown_as: one bank sits in a blue band beside four borrowers, each wearing a different % tag (5, 15, 12, 3); a PLR heading gets a pointer label, a definition line writes on underneath, then a red 'issues' label opens two cream chips for missing transparency and standardisation; the top strip gains a 1973 tick
segments.example: four borrowers of one bank at 5%, 15%, 12%, 3%

segments.teaches: in 2003 BPLR replaced PLR: the rate a bank charges its most creditworthy customer, taken as the minimum interest

elements.what: the 1973-2003 span on the strip is named prime lending rate; a dotted line drops from the 2003 tick to the new heading
BPLR with its full name under a rule
short definition; 'most creditworthy customer' highlighted blue
arrow from the highlighted phrase to a person icon
bank building and person
diagonal loan arrow from bank up to the person with a % marker on it
curved pointer from the % to 'minimum interest'

segments.notes: 8 change events (~every 7 s). The dotted drop line from a timeline tick to each new heading is a reusable 'era anchor'.
segments.idea: BPLR is the rate for a bank's safest borrower, so it acts as the lowest rate the bank should charge
segments.shown_as: the top strip's 1973-2003 span gets the PLR name and a dotted line drops from 2003 to a BPLR heading; in the definition the 'most creditworthy customer' phrase is highlighted and an arrow carries it to a person icon; then a diagonal loan arrow from the bank to that person gets a % marker with a 'minimum interest' pointer

segments.teaches: BPLR was fixed for banks under RBI's direction and treated as the minimum interest, meant to bring transparency and standardisation

elements.what: pink box under the BPLR heading holding four bank icons, later a red [FIXED] tag on top
RBI emblem coin with the letters RBI, below the box
four dotted arrows fanning from the RBI coin up to the four banks
wavy brace beside RBI opening to 'BPLR = minimum interest'
two cream goal chips: transparency, standardisation

segments.notes: 4 change events (~every 12 s). Regulator below, banks above, dotted 'direction' arrows going up: RBI's rule pushed into a group of banks. The two goal chips are planted here so they can be crossed out later.
segments.idea: RBI made banks fix a BPLR and treat it as the floor, expecting clear and uniform loan pricing
segments.shown_as: four bank icons sit in a pink box under the BPLR heading; the RBI coin appears below and four dotted arrows rise from it to the banks, then a red [FIXED] tag lands on the box; beside RBI a wavy brace opens to 'BPLR = minimum interest' and two goal chips

segments.teaches: a 2010 review found 77% of lending below BPLR because banks competed for customers; the 'minimum' was only an assumption and both goals failed

elements.what: 2010 tick added to the top strip
report document with an orange tick, hanging from the 2010 tick
arrow from the report to 'total lending below BPLR = 77%'
red 'but why?' line
short reason: banks competing to win customers
red strike through 'BPLR = minimum interest' with a red 'only an assumption' label
red crosses under the transparency and standardisation chips

segments.notes: 5 change events in 116 s (~every 23 s): the slowest stretch. At about 329 the notes clear and only the bare BPLR box remains. Good device: goals planted as chips, crossed when the evidence arrives. Weak: the 77% is only text; BIE could slide 77 of 100 loan tokens below a BPLR floor line.
segments.idea: banks undercut each other, so most loans went below the supposed floor and the reform failed its two goals
segments.shown_as: a 2010 tick and a ticked report icon drop onto the top strip; an arrow from the report writes '77% of lending below BPLR'; a red 'but why?' is answered by a short reason line; then the 'BPLR = minimum interest' line is struck in red with 'only an assumption', and red crosses land under the two goal chips
segments.example: 2010: 77% of total bank lending below BPLR

segments.teaches: in 2010 the base rate replaced BPLR: a floor below which a bank cannot lend, which each bank sets for itself; interest rates deregulated

elements.what: BASE RATE heading under the 2010 tick; the BPLR heading moves aside
floor definition replaces the [FIXED] tag inside the pink box
gold ring around one of the four banks, pointer to 'banks set their own base rate'
dotted arrows between banks and the RBI coin, now pointing down to RBI
caption under RBI: interest rates deregulated

segments.notes: 8 change events (~every 5 s): the busiest part. The same box-and-arrows picture is reused for BPLR and base rate; only the tag, the gold ring and the arrow direction change, so the viewer sees exactly what changed.
segments.idea: the base rate is a floor that each bank works out for itself; RBI no longer fixes it
segments.shown_as: the BPLR heading slides aside and BASE RATE drops from the new 2010 tick; the pink box's [FIXED] tag gives way to the floor definition; one of the four banks is ringed in gold with a pointer saying banks set their own; the dotted arrows now run from the banks down to the RBI coin, and a 'rates deregulated' caption appears under RBI

segments.teaches: a bank builds its base rate from cost of funds, operating expenses, a minimum return and the cost of keeping CRR, which restores transparency and standardisation

elements.what: 'base rate calculation' list of four cost parts with square bullets
blue band over the bullet being discussed (operating expenses)
transparency and standardisation chips return beside the box behind a wavy brace
blue ticks after both chips
2015 tick appears on the top strip as a teaser for the next system

segments.notes: 3 change events before the reset at about 421. The red-cross -> blue-tick reversal on the same two chips is a strong 'problem fixed' device. Weak: the four parts are a list; they could be stacked blocks adding up to the base-rate height.
segments.idea: each bank's floor rate is built from its own costs plus a minimum return, so it can be explained and compared
segments.shown_as: a four-line calculation list (fund cost, running cost, minimum return, CRR cost) writes on beside the ringed bank and one line is lit while spoken; the transparency and standardisation chips come back beside the box and each gets a blue tick, reversing the earlier red crosses; a 2015 tick appears on the strip

segments.teaches: channel end card (next video / playlist); not teaching

elements.what: next-video and playlist panels with bird illustrations

segments.shown_as: canvas clears to a two-panel channel end card
